criteria.name: Introduction — Identifies ethical issues and broad links to engineering design; discusses the context of ethical issues in engineering organisations; identifies relevant stakeholders when considering the ethical issues.
criteria.reasoning: Identifies multiple ethical issues in engineering design, thoroughly explaining organisational context and mapping out stakeholder interests comprehensively in Table 1.

criteria.name: Balanced Discussion — Discusses objective arguments for and against decisions on the ethical issues; draws a conclusion on how stakeholders should make decisions about the issues.
criteria.reasoning: Balanced, deep objective arguments for and against shipping are presented, culminating in clear, actionable recommendations across multiple stakeholder groups.

evidence.quote: Deploying at scale would give the product engineers the field data they need to make safety improvements before the larger international contracts.
Rachel should withhold quality sign-off for the health contract, record the untested failure modes in writing and escalate to management.

criteria.name: Compelling Argument that supports conclusion — The report forms a compelling argument that justifies the conclusion; the body follows a logical structure, with linked paragraphs and content ordered to support the argument; arguments demonstrate a systematic understanding of the ethical issues for all stakeholders.
criteria.reasoning: The argument forms a compelling, coherent narrative that systematically evaluates trade-offs and rigorously justifies the conclusions and options.

evidence.quote: Options B and C respect every stakeholder's interests better than either extreme.

criteria.name: Research and Evidence — Arguments are substantiated with adequate references and qualitative/quantitative evidence; research demonstrates a balanced, in-depth understanding of the topic.
criteria.reasoning: Substantiated with high-quality references and both qualitative and quantitative real-world case evidence (WannaCry, Therac-25, Intel Pentium, VW emissions).

criteria.reasoning: Flawlessly structured report featuring fluent language, well-formatted tables, an effective decision flowchart (Figure 1), and pristine IEEE citations.

overall: An exceptional, professional-grade engineering ethics report. It provides deep, balanced ethical analysis supported by pertinent empirical case studies, clear visual decision models, and well-targeted recommendations.

feedback.summary: You have produced an exceptional, professional-grade ethics report that achieved top marks across all criteria. Your analysis was rigorous and balanced, supported by excellent real-world evidence, well-crafted visual models, and clear stakeholder mapping. To sustain this outstanding standard in future technical reports, focus on maintaining your methodical approach to stakeholder trade-offs, empirical evidence integration, and concise visual communication.
next_steps: Apply the structured decision-tree methodology used in Figure 1 to future risk assessment tasks.
Continue incorporating quantitative historical case studies to substantiate engineering ethics and design decisions.
Maintain the clear, multi-tiered stakeholder recommendation framework developed in your final section across future engineering management reports.

criteria.C1: You achieved the Excellent standard by clearly framing ethical design issues within their organisational contexts. In the Introduction and Table 1, you comprehensively mapped how calendar-driven test coverage directly impacts stakeholders, particularly vulnerable groups like patients and clinicians. To sustain this level, continue to explicitly link technical workflow constraints to external human consequences.
criteria.C2: You reached the Excellent standard by providing deep, objective arguments both for and against shipping. Your sections balanced engineering field-data requirements with risk mitigation, leading to nuanced, actionable recommendations for Rachel, management, and clients. Keep integrating distinct stakeholder perspectives to ensure decisions are multi-dimensional and fully justified.
criteria.C3: You met the Excellent criteria with a compelling, coherent narrative that logically bridges your analysis and final proposals. In 'The Most Ethical Path', you systematically evaluated trade-offs between extreme choices, providing a fully justified compromise. Continue structuring arguments around balanced intermediate options to maintain persuasive, evidence-based conclusions.
criteria.C4: You demonstrated an Excellent standard through exemplary research combining qualitative and quantitative evidence. Citing concrete real-world cases—such as the 19,000 cancelled NHS appointments during WannaCry and Intel’s US$475 million charge—powerfully grounded your ethical claims. Retain this practice of pairing ethical theory with measurable historical outcomes.
criteria.C5: You achieved Excellent marks with a flawlessly structured report, sophisticated prose, and immaculate IEEE referencing. Visual tools like Table 1 and the Figure 1 decision flowchart effectively reinforced your written analysis. Continue using clear visual artefacts and professional technical formatting to support complex arguments in future work.
